311: Endnotes continue. Note 7: The doors Carnegie opened for Napoleon Hill would lead to more than two decades of study and face-to-face discussions with an almost unbelievable array of business, professional, and public leaders and philanthropists, including four Presidents of the United States. The editor provides additional biographical details about many of these individuals. WILLIAM WRIGLEY, JR. (1861-1932): at age 13, was a traveling salesman for his father's soap company. In 1891 he peddled soap with baking powder as a sales premium. In 1892 he began selling baking powder with chewing gum as a premium. The response was so good he dropped the soap and baking powder to focus exclusively on selling gum, eventually making 'Wrigley's' a familiar name. He pioneered sales incentives, offering dealers clocks, coffee grinders, and fishing tackle. In 1893 he introduced Wrigley's Spearmint Gum. By 1908 sales had hit $1 million per year.
312: Endnotes continue with biographical details. JOHN WANAMAKER (1838-1922): In 1875 he bought a freight depot from the Pennsylvania Railroad to house his new sales operation, featuring specialty shops under one roof—a new kind of 'department' store. He became one of the first retailers to employ an advertising agency. He also served as Postmaster General of the United States under President Benjamin Harrison. GEORGE S. PARKER (1867-1953): At age 16, established his own game publishing company. By 1888, Parker Brothers was created with his brother Charles. George wrote the rules for all games they produced. In 1935, the company introduced Monopoly. In all, George Parker invented more than 100 games. E. M. STATLER (1863-1928): His hotels were the first to have running water and private baths in each room. By the mid-1920s, the Statler properties were the largest in America owned by a single individual. His company slogan: 'The customer is always right.' HENRY L. DOHERTY (1870-1939): In 1910 organized and became president of Cities Services Company, a holding company for more than 100 public utilities and petroleum businesses with total assets exceeding $1 billion ($17 billion in today's dollars).
313: Endnotes continue. CYRUS H. K. CURTIS (1850-1933): Founded Tribune and Farmer in Philadelphia in 1876 with his wife Louise Knapp Curtis in charge of the women's column. The latter was so popular he expanded it into Ladies' Home Journal in 1883. He established Curtis Publishing Company in 1890 and seven years later bought The Saturday Evening Post for $1,000. Both magazines became two of the biggest success stories in periodical history. GEORGE EASTMAN (1854-1932): His hand-held Kodak camera and $1 Brownie Camera for kids opened photography to the masses. In 1924 he gave away half his fortune, about $75 million, for institutions including the University of Rochester and MIT. He was the first large-scale manufacturer to use profit sharing as an employee benefit. JOHN W. DAVIS (1873-1955): Served as Solicitor General of the United States, Ambassador to Great Britain, and as advisor to Woodrow Wilson at the Paris Peace Conference. In 1952 he won a landmark Supreme Court case convincing the Court that President Harry Truman had exceeded his constitutional powers in seizing the steel mills. WILBUR WRIGHT (1867-1912): Got the idea for the design of his and brother Orville's aircraft after watching buzzards flying, realizing an airplane must be capable of moving on three axes. WILLIAM JENNINGS BRYAN (1860-1925): A silver-tongued orator who served as prosecuting attorney in the Scopes Monkey Trial, squared off against Clarence Darrow.
314: Endnotes continue. DR. DAVID STARR JORDAN (1851-1931): The world's foremost scientific authority on fish, naming more than 2,500 species. After his tenure as Stanford's president, he served as chief director of the World Peace Foundation. DANIEL WILLARD (1861-1942): In addition to railroad responsibilities, served as member of the Board of Visitors of the U.S. Naval Academy and as chairman of the War Industries Board in 1917. KING GILLETTE (1855-1932): On a trip as a traveling hardware salesman, was advised to invent 'something that would be used and thrown away.' The idea of a thin double-edged steel razor blade in a T-handle flashed into his mind. In 1903 he sold 51 razors and 168 blades. By the end of 1904, his company had sold 90,000 razors and 12.4 million blades. JOHN D. ROCKEFELLER (1839-1937): Standard Oil Company dominated the oil industry and was America's first great business trust. By 1910 his fortune was equal to almost 2.5 percent of the entire U.S. economy—about $250 billion in today's dollars. In 1911 the courts broke up Standard Oil into several companies (Esso/EXXON, Mobil, Chevron, Amoco, Standard Oil of Ohio). His donations made possible the founding of the University of Chicago, Rockefeller University, and the Rockefeller Foundation. He gave away $500 million during his lifetime; total charitable gifts with his son amounted to $2.5 billion by 1955.
315: Endnotes continue. FRANK A. VANDERLIP (1864-1937): A financial reporter and later financial editor of the Chicago Tribune prior to becoming a banker. Served as chairman of the War Savings Committee for World War I and was a trustee of the Carnegie Foundation. F. W. WOOLWORTH (1852-1919): Opened his first five-and-ten-cent variety store in 1879 in Lancaster, Pennsylvania. By the end of 1904, he was operating 120 stores in 21 states, and by his death the company had more than a thousand stores. He pioneered volume buying and artful counter display merchandising. By the late 1990s the chain had lost a long battle against big discounters, and in 1997 the Woolworth Corporation announced it was closing its last 400 stores with 9,000 employees. COL. ROBERT A. DOLLAR (1844-1932): Born in Falkirk, Scotland, immigrated to the United States in 1856. By age 13 he was working in a Canadian lumber camp. He made his way to San Francisco and developed extensive foreign trading and lumber businesses, becoming one of the largest operators of ocean vessels in the world. Before his death, he had received keys to the cities of Falkirk, Boston, New York, and Shanghai. EDWARD A. FILENE (1860-1937): Along with brother Lincoln, made Filene's department store in Boston world-famous. Known for its Automatic Bargain Basement, which opened in 1909, featuring distressed merchandise at automatically reducing prices. Filene's pioneered the charge-plate system, cycle billing, and branch store operations.
316: Endnotes continue. Filene's joined with F. & R. Lazarus and Company and Abraham and Strauss in 1929 to form Federated Department Stores, Inc. Edward Filene was co-inventor of the 'Filene-Finlay Simultaneous Translator,' used at the Nuremberg war crimes trials and later at the United Nations. Because of his 30-year crusade to establish credit unions in the United States, Filene is known as the 'Father of the U.S. Credit Union Movement.' ARTHUR BRISBANE (1864-1936): The highest paid newspaper editor in the United States and one of the world's most widely read editorialists, as managing editor of William Randolph Hearst's The New York Evening Journal. Known as the master of sensationalism, he wrote the syndicated 'Today' editorial column from 1917 until his death in 1936. He also campaigned for better schools, labor law, prison reform, and against the death penalty, crime, and Prohibition. LUTHER BURBANK (1849-1926): During a horticultural career lasting 55 years, developed more than 800 varieties and strains of plants, including more than 200 varieties of fruits (including the Freestone peach). In 1871 he developed the Burbank potato, used in Ireland against the blight epidemic. He was a friend of both Thomas Edison and Henry Ford. EDWARD W. BOK (1863-1930): Edited Ladies Home Journal for three decades. His greatest crusade was against the excesses of the patent medicine industry, which led to passage of the Pure Food and Drug Act in 1906. Ladies Home Journal was the first American magazine to mention venereal disease. Bok won the 1921 Pulitzer Prize for his autobiography, The Americanization of Edward Bok.
317: Endnotes continue. FRANK A. MUNSEY (1854-1925): A master of media consolidation and mergers. Published America's first inexpensive (10 cents per copy) general circulation, illustrated magazine, Munsey's Magazine. At his death, he left most of his $40 million (more than $412 million in today's dollars) to the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City. JULIUS ROSENWALD (1862-1932): A clothing merchant who bought a one-quarter interest in Sears, Roebuck and Company, becoming its president in 1910 and chairman in 1925. Under his leadership, Sears began manufacturing its own products and established the 'satisfaction guaranteed or your money back' policy. He objected to 'perpetual endowments,' advocating 'matched giving' instead. One of his bequests led to the establishment of 5,000 schools in 15 Southern states for the education of blacks. He also established the Museum of Science and Industry in Chicago. CLARENCE DARROW (1857-1938): After nine years as a small-town lawyer in Ohio, relocated to Chicago. His liberal views led him to take famous cases including the Leopold-Loeb Case (saving two men from the death penalty), the Sweet Case (defending a black family in Detroit), and the Scopes 'Monkey Trial' where he squared off against William Jennings Bryan. Despite the widespread view that Darrow had won the contest, Scopes was found guilty.
318: Endnotes continue. JENNINGS RANDOLPH (1902-1998): Graduated from Salem College in 1924. Like Napoleon Hill, he worked as a journalist. He served seven terms as U.S. Congressman from West Virginia (1933 to 1947) and four full terms as U.S. Senator (1958 to 1985). Fondly remembered as 'the last of the New Deal Democrats,' he gained renown as chairman of the Senate's Public Works Committee and was the legislative father of the National Air and Space Museum in Washington, D.C. Senator Robert C. Byrd recalled Randolph's love of flight, describing how on November 6, 1948, Randolph flew from Morgantown, West Virginia, to Washington National Airport in a propeller plane fueled with gasoline made from coal—'an act of faith.' Randolph authored the 26th Amendment to the Constitution giving 18-year-olds the right to vote. He was considered the father of the Appalachian Regional Commission. He served for many years as a member of the Board of Directors of the Napoleon Hill Foundation, established in 1962 by Hill and his wife Annie Lou. Randolph died of pneumonia at age 96 on May 8, 1998. He had the distinction of being the last surviving person (non-Hill family member) mentioned by name in the original 1937 edition of Think and Grow Rich!

Note 3: The notion of 'transmutation'—literally, the process by which some object is changed into another nature, form, or condition—is crucial to understanding Hill's philosophy of success. Hill uses the term to describe the process by which intangible thought is translated into physical activity that results in a physical change in the world. He also uses it to describe converting one kind of mental state into another. Note 4: Edwin C. Barnes was born in Jefferson City, Wisconsin, in 1876 and died at age 78 in Bradentown (now Bradenton), Florida, in 1954. His relationship with the Edison organization made him independently wealthy.
320: Endnotes continue. Barnes moved to Bradenton from Chicago during the building boom of the 1920s and became the primary developer of the luxurious Palma Sola Park subdivision. An article in the August 21, 1924, edition of the Manatee River Journal-Herald gives a hint of the close relationship between Barnes and Edison until the latter's death in 1931: 'Edwin C. Barnes of Bradentown and Chicago broke into the front page of the New York Times in company with Thomas Edison the other day. The immaculate Edwin demonstrated that he could kick a hat held shoulder high, and Mr. Edison, who is Mr. Barnes' senior by about thirty-five years, demonstrated that he could do the same thing. Mr. Barnes has for years been connected with the Edison organization and he and the wizard are close friends. They have another interest in common—their love for Florida.' Barnes was also a long-time and close friend of Napoleon Hill. Hill dedicated his book Law of Success to three persons—Andrew Carnegie, Henry Ford, and Edwin C. Barnes. Note 5: An uncle of R. U. Note 6: William Rainey Harper (1856-1906) was the first president of the University of Chicago, leaving a post as professor of semitic languages at Yale University. He was an innovator who initiated extension courses, studies in new disciplines such as psychology and sociology, and was instrumental in establishing junior colleges.
